planting.note: Tuck rhizome divisions into gritty, calcareous, well-drained soil among rocks or on a shaded slope in spring.

directions: Tuck rhizome divisions into gritty, calcareous, well-drained soil among rocks or on a shaded slope in spring, mimicking the cool talus and cliff-base habitats this circumboreal alpine fern favors from Alaska south through the Rockies. Its stiff, once-pinnate fronds with holly-like spiny-toothed pinnae form a tight evergreen rosette that holds its dark green color through harsh winters, making it a striking accent for shaded rock gardens and cold-climate crevice plantings. It resents summer heat and humidity, so it performs best in northern and high-elevation gardens with excellent drainage and consistent but not soggy moisture.

planting.note: Plant divisions or containers in fall or early spring in fast-draining, rocky to loamy soil beneath conifers or on shaded slopes.

directions: Plant divisions or containers in fall or early spring in fast-draining, rocky to loamy soil beneath conifers or on shaded slopes, where this Pacific Coast native tolerates far drier conditions than its larger relative western sword fern. The narrow, leathery, once-pinnate fronds form dense upright clumps and hold their deep green color year-round, offering reliable texture beneath oaks and pines where summer irrigation is minimal. It is especially valuable for dry-shade woodland gardens from southern Oregon through California.

planting.note: Set out divisions in fall in humus-rich to rocky soil on shaded coastal bluffs, canyon walls, or slopes.

directions: Set out divisions in fall in humus-rich to rocky soil on shaded coastal bluffs, canyon walls, or slopes, including serpentine sites where this California and southern Oregon native is often found growing wild. Its compact, evergreen, once-pinnate fronds with prominent basal auricles form neat clumps that stay attractive through the dry summer once roots are established. A dependable, low-maintenance choice for coastal and foothill shade gardens that receive little supplemental water after the first year.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in rich, moisture-retentive soil beneath redwoods, oaks, or other coastal forest canopy.

directions: Plant divisions in fall in rich, moisture-retentive soil beneath redwoods, oaks, or other coastal forest canopy, since this California endemic naturally forms the lush fern understory of Coast Range mixed-evergreen woodlands. The broadly triangular, bipinnate fronds are a brighter, softer green than most sword ferns and arch gracefully from a slowly expanding crown, giving a fuller, lacier look than western sword fern. It is an excellent structural anchor for shaded native gardens that receive regular winter rain and light summer watering.
